results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All ten outline summaries state the controlling idea of the spec paragraph they are aligned to (p01-p10); the callout is page format.

Introduction ¶3 holds thesis statement and roadmap, which is p03's single controlling idea by design. Chapters in this part ¶2 holds synthesis, callback, reading advice and hand-off, all assigned to p10 and the conclusion by the spec. Neither holds an idea beyond its spec entry.
Lead and test paragraph set up all three claims; type list traces to P2-1, modes to P2-2, size to P2-3, the order paragraph to all three; the closing units restate them as chapters.

Each Corvane scenario is followed by what it shows (the wait, the two open questions, size chosen first); Team Topologies and An Elegant Puzzle are named with what Part II does with them; the type list and chapter list each have a lead-in that says what the items share. Larson's on-call figure (about eight) is not given, which is not required.

results.draft_locus: Three Choices: Type, Mode and Size ¶1
results.quote: The first choice is what a team is for.
results.finding: The spec asks for a sentence at the start of the section that carries over the two-question test and presents the three choices as what it is applied to (relationship: example). The opening sentence names the first choice and does not mention the test or that three choices follow from it; the test reappears only in the third sentence, for types alone. All other declared transitions (p02, p03, the-test, p06, p07, p08, the conclusion, p10) and the hand-off to team-types read as declared.

results.draft_locus: The Test: Whose Load, Whose Waiting ¶1
results.quote: Any other team, and any dependency between teams, therefore has to answer two questions.
results.finding: Two different pairs are both called 'two questions': kind of team / how others use it in the lead ('Part II answers those two questions for every team.') and whose load / whose waiting in the test. Both flow readers went back to the lead to confirm the pairs differ. The prose can name the pairs differently (for example keep 'the test' for load and waiting) without changing the spec's order.

results.draft_locus: Three Choices: Type, Mode and Size ¶2

results.finding: Platform team, cognitive load, the four types, interaction modes and each mode, team API and on-call rotation are each glossed where they first appear; six to eight is attributed to Larson and its origin left to chapter 8 as the spec says. 'Mode' is used once in the roadmap before 'interaction modes' is introduced, after 'three ways for two teams to work together'; both flow readers resolved it from context (b), trivial.
Opens on a specific dated scenario with numbers; no placeholder, restated question, definition or broad-history opening.

The closing synthesizes, calls back, advises and hands off. The Corvane sentence repeats the previous paragraph's point (both flow readers found it repetitive) but it is the spec's callback, not new body evidence.

results.quote: If you arrive with one question about a team, open the chapter that answers it; otherwise read in order.
results.finding: The synthesis is there (one question from three sides). The so-what is not: the closing does not say that the reader can test every team with the two questions and refuse a team or dependency that answers neither; that appears only in the test section ('a leader can refuse it'). The second half of the synthesis (a staffing complaint becomes three design decisions) is also absent. Fault is unclear because p10's controlling idea in the spec does not include the so-what that /conclusion/so_what asks for, and the paragraph already carries four jobs.

results.finding: The closing returns to Corvane's platform team of five and its 2022 plan: first two questions unanswered, the third answered with a bare number.
The intro reader predicted the test (whose load, whose waiting), then the three choices in dependency order, then the three chapters and their questions: both roadmap promises.
The reader named team types; interaction modes and team APIs; team size and composition, in order, matching the expected answer. The reader noted the page says little about what 'composition' covers.
